concerns.text: The plan generates synthetic BOLD time‑series using noise estimates derived from the real datasets (step 3). Relying on simulated data may not capture the full complexity of true neuroimaging signals (e.g., physiological noise, motion artefacts, inter‑subject variability), which limits the external/construct validity of the resulting power curves.

Split‑half validation is performed on the same synthetic dataset (step 4). Because both halves share the same underlying noise model and simulated signal, this does not constitute an independent replication test and may produce overly optimistic power estimates.

Replication success is defined as matching direction **and** magnitude within ±20 % of the training estimate (plus p < α). The ±20 % tolerance is arbitrary and not justified; it could substantially affect the estimated replication probability and should be either theoretically motivated or explored via sensitivity analysis.

The logistic regression model assumes predictors (sample size, smoothing kernel, SNR) are orthogonal by design, yet no empirical check is shown. In practice sample size and SNR may be correlated (larger samples often have higher SNR). Relying on VIF < 5 without demonstrating orthogonality risks multicollinearity bias.

Only four sample‑size points per paradigm (10, 20, 40, 60) are evaluated. This sparse grid may be insufficient to reliably capture the non‑linear relationship between sample size and replication probability, especially at the lower end where power curves typically change steeply.
